analysis.one_liner: Bans data brokers from selling people's health and location data.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Elizabeth Warren with five Democratic-aligned cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for data brokers — companies that buy and resell information about individuals — to sell, trade, or share data showing where a person is or has been, or data revealing their health conditions, including pregnancy and miscarriage. It would put enforcement in the hands of the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and private individuals, with penalties of up to 15 percent of a company's parent company's annual revenue. It carves out HIPAA-compliant health information, news reporting, and data a person explicitly authorizes to be shared. The bill was referred to committee and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who carries a phone or uses the internet — essentially everyone — gains protection against the sale of their health and location information. People seeking reproductive health care, people with mental health or disability histories, and people whose movements (visits to clinics, places of worship, protests) could be inferred from location data stand to gain the most, since the bill's definition of health data explicitly includes pregnancy and miscarriage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose phone or health data is sold

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits data brokers from selling, licensing, trading, or sharing any individual's location data or health data, including data about pregnancy, miscarriage, disability, and mental health.

Gives the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and private individuals the power to sue violators, with civil penalties of up to 15 percent of the violator's ultimate parent company's revenues from the prior 12 months.

Preserves HIPAA-compliant handling of health information by covered entities and business associates, plus news publication and disclosures the individual authorizes, so routine medical and journalistic uses are not disrupted.
Appropriates $1 billion to the FTC to carry out the law through fiscal year 2032.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the app and advertising companies that profit from monetizing people's health and location information lose a revenue stream. Some apps that are free because they sell user data might begin charging or showing more ads. Compliance and litigation exposure would fall on any company trafficking in this data.

drawbacks.text: The bill restricts only the sale and transfer of data by brokers — not the original collection — so the apps and services that gather health and location data could still keep it in-house, limiting how much the bill actually reduces data exposure.

The definition of regulated data is very broad — anything 'reasonably linkable' to a person or even to a group sharing an IP address — and the bill creates a private right of action with attorney's fees, which could generate extensive litigation for companies trying to comply in good faith.
The $1 billion appropriation to the FTC is a substantial new federal expenditure, and the rulemaking deadline of 180 days is aggressive for the scope of the rules required.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — keeping health and location data out of the brokerage market — addresses a real harm that ordinary people cannot protect themselves against, since data sales are invisible and unavoidable for anyone using a phone. The design has rough edges: it leaves collection untouched, relies on sweeping definitions, and adds a large new enforcement appropriation. On balance, the benefit to personal privacy outweighs those design flaws, which is likely why the industry-facing cost rather than the drafting details determined its fate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which took no further action on it before the Congress ended, so it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on June 15, 2022, with original cosponsors including Sens. Wyden, Murray, Whitehouse, and Sanders.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced.
The committee's action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; the last recorded action is the referral on June 15, 2022.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the advertising-technology companies that buy and resell people's health and location data are better off, because the revenue stream the bill would have shut down continued uninterrupted. Phone users gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit data brokers from selling health and location data.

for.name: Sens. Wyden, Murray, Whitehouse, and Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee action during the remainder of the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; none of the Senate's 50 Republicans cosponsored, and the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: These companies buy and resell information about individuals; the bill would outlaw their trade in health and location data entirely, with penalties up to 15 percent of parent-company revenue. Their business model depends on monetizing data people never knowingly sold.

Location data sold by brokers feeds much of mobile targeted advertising, so cutting off the supply of location data shrinks a major input to the ad market. Consumers currently bear this cost as surveillance they cannot opt out of.

industries.industry: Health, pregnancy, and fitness app makers
industries.note: Apps that collect health and location data and monetize it through brokers would lose that revenue; apps that never sell data would face little change. Users of these apps currently cannot tell which kind they are using.
